tool.name: Laravel
tool.tagline: Batteries-included PHP framework for web apps and APIs
tool.description: Laravel is the most popular PHP web framework, with an expressive routing layer, the Eloquent ORM, Blade templates, queues, events and first-class testing. It favours convention and developer experience, and its ecosystem (Sanctum, Horizon, Octane, Reverb, Forge, Cloud) covers most of what a product team needs. Learning it is the fastest way to build and ship production PHP applications.

glossary.def: A ready-made set of Laravel login, sign-up and password-reset pages you can add when creating a project.
Laravel's command-line tool, run as php artisan. It generates code, runs migrations, starts a development server and much more.
Laravel's interactive prompt (php artisan tinker): type a line of PHP and see the result at once, with your app and database ready to use.
In Laravel, a rule that connects an HTTP method and a URL, such as GET /posts, to the code that answers it.
A Laravel route given a name, like posts.show, so code can build its URL with route() instead of typing the path.
One Laravel line, Route::resource(), that registers the seven standard routes for listing, showing, creating, editing and deleting one kind of record.
Laravel loading a database record for you from a URL part, such as the {user} in /users/{user}, or answering 404 if it doesn't exist.
In Laravel, a class whose methods answer the requests for one part of the app, such as PostController for blog posts.
Data Laravel keeps in the session for the next request only, used for one-off messages like 'Saved!' after a redirect.
Laravel's template language: HTML files with {{ }} for printing values and @ commands such as @if and @foreach.
A Blade command starting with @, such as @if, @foreach or @csrf, that Laravel turns into PHP.
A reusable piece of a Blade page, used like an HTML tag such as <x-alert>, with its own template and optional PHP class.
The content placed between a Blade component's opening and closing tags, which the component prints with {{ $slot }}.
Laravel's PHP way of describing tables and columns (Schema::create, $table->string(...)), which it turns into the right SQL for your database.
A Laravel class that fills the database with starting or sample data, run with php artisan db:seed.
A Laravel class that makes realistic fake records of one model, for sample data and tests: User::factory()->create().
Laravel's ORM: each database table gets a PHP model class, and rows come back as objects you can read, change and save.
In Laravel, a class such as Post that stands for one database table; each object of it is one row.
Laravel's chainable methods, like where()->orderBy()->get(), that build an SQL query step by step and run it.
Laravel's wrapper around a PHP array with many chainable methods such as map, filter and pluck. Eloquent queries return them.
Filling many model columns at once from an array, as Model::create($data) does. Laravel only allows the columns you list in $fillable.
A Laravel model setting that converts a column's value to a PHP type when read, such as text into a date object or JSON into an array.
A Laravel class holding the validation rules and permission check for one kind of request; Laravel runs it before your controller method.
Telling Eloquent up front which related records you'll need, so it fetches them all in one extra query instead of one query per record.
In Laravel, the table that links two models in a many-to-many relationship, holding pairs of ids, such as post_tag.
An Eloquent relationship where one model can belong to several kinds of model, such as comments on both posts and videos.
In Laravel, a named permission check written as a function, such as 'view-reports', for rules not tied to one model.
A Laravel class that holds the permission rules for one model, such as PostPolicy::update deciding who may edit a post.
Laravel's package for logging in API clients: it issues tokens to mobile apps and can use normal cookie login for your own JavaScript front end.
In Laravel, the service container: the object that builds your classes and everything their constructors ask for, following bindings you register.
A rule registered in Laravel's container saying how to build something, such as which class to create when an interface is asked for.
The container building a class without any setup, by reading its constructor's parameter types and building each of those too.
A Laravel class that sets the app up as it starts: register() adds container bindings and boot() does setup that needs other services.
In Laravel, starting the application: loading configuration and running every service provider's boot() method so all services are ready.
In Laravel, the object that takes each request through start-up, the middleware and the router, and returns the response.
A Laravel class like Cache or Mail whose static-looking calls are passed to a service fetched from the container.
In Laravel, a method you add to a core class such as Collection or Str at runtime with ::macro(), usually in a service provider.
In Laravel, a class describing one piece of work to run later on a queue, with a handle() method that does it.
Laravel's dashboard and manager for Redis queues: shows job throughput and failures and balances workers.
In Laravel, a small class announcing that something happened, such as OrderShipped, which listeners then react to.
A Laravel class whose handle() method runs when a particular event is dispatched.
A Laravel class grouping the methods that react to one model's events, such as created or deleted.
An event Eloquent fires automatically when a model is created, updated, saved or deleted.
A Laravel test that starts the whole app and sends it a fake HTTP request, then checks the response and the database.
A Laravel test stand-in, such as Queue::fake() or Mail::fake(), that records what your code tried to do instead of doing it.
A PHP testing framework built on PHPUnit with a shorter, function-based style; Laravel supports it out of the box.
A Laravel class that turns a model into exactly the JSON an API should return, independent of the database columns.
A Laravel package that runs the app in long-lived worker processes, so it starts once and then handles many requests, much faster.
A Laravel state, switched on with php artisan down, in which visitors see a 'back soon' page while you update the site.
Combining all Laravel configuration into one cached file (php artisan config:cache) for speed; .env is then no longer read.

concepts.name: Project setup and structure
concepts.summary: Create a Laravel 12 project, run it on your computer and learn what lives in each top-level folder.
concepts.why: Knowing where things go is the first step to navigating any Laravel codebase.
concepts.body:
Laravel is a **framework** for building websites in PHP: a large, ready-made structure where you fill in your own parts and it decides when to call them. It handles the chores every site needs — reading requests, talking to the database, building pages — so you write only what's special about your app.

Create a project with the Laravel installer, `laravel new example-app`, or with Composer, `composer create-project laravel/laravel example-app`. The installer can add a **starter kit**: ready-made login and sign-up pages, built with the JavaScript tool of your choice (React, Vue or Livewire). New apps keep their data in SQLite, a database stored in a single file, so they work with no database setup.

Run `php artisan serve` to start a development web server, then open `http://localhost:8000` in your browser. `composer run dev` starts the server plus a few helpers at once, such as Vite, which rebuilds your page styles (CSS) and JavaScript as you edit them.

The folders:
- `app/`: your own PHP classes, autoloaded under the `App\` namespace.
- `routes/`: `web.php` lists which **URL** (web address, such as `/posts/5`) runs which code. (`console.php` holds your own commands; `api.php` is added later with `php artisan install:api`.)
- `resources/`: your page **templates** (HTML with blanks for your data), CSS and JavaScript.
- `database/`: migrations, plus classes that fill the database with sample data.

- `config/`: settings files, one per topic (`database.php`, `mail.php`...).
- `bootstrap/app.php`: wires the app together, for example which **middleware** to use (code that runs before and after every request, such as a login check).
- `public/index.php`: the one file the web server runs; every request goes through it.
- `storage/`: logs, uploaded files and files Laravel generates; `tests/`: your automated tests.

Settings that differ between your laptop and the live site, such as the database password, go in a file called `.env`, which is never committed to Git. Your code reads them through the files in `config/`.

**Artisan** is Laravel's command-line tool, a program you use by typing commands in the terminal: `php artisan list` shows everything it can do. It generates code (`make:controller`, `make:model`), runs migrations, and opens **Tinker**, where you type a line of PHP and see the result immediately, with your app loaded.
concepts.code:
laravel new example-app          # or: composer create-project laravel/laravel example-app
cd example-app
composer run dev                 # dev server and helpers in one terminal
# or just: php artisan serve     -> http://127.0.0.1:8000

php artisan --version            # Laravel Framework 12.x
php artisan about                # overview of your app's settings
php artisan list make            # all code generators

php artisan make:controller PostController
php artisan make:model Post --migration --factory
php artisan tinker               # interactive PHP prompt with your app loaded
# > App\Models\User::count()
takeaways: Create apps with laravel new or composer create-project
public/index.php receives every request; your own code lives in app/
Use php artisan to generate code, run migrations and open Tinker
pitfalls: Committing .env with real passwords; only .env.example belongs in Git.

quiz.q: Where is middleware configured in a fresh Laravel 12 app?
quiz.explain: Since Laravel 11, bootstrap/app.php configures middleware, routes and error handling; the old app/Http/Kernel.php no longer exists.

concepts.name: Routing
concepts.summary: Connect URLs to code with Route::get and friends, route parameters, named routes and resource routes.
concepts.why: Routes are the front door of every Laravel app: they decide which code answers each URL.
concepts.body:
A **route** connects a URL and an **HTTP method** (GET to read a page, POST to submit a form, and so on) to the code that answers it. Deciding which code runs for each request is called **routing**.

Routes for web pages live in `routes/web.php`. The simplest route returns a value directly:

```php
Route::get('/hello', fn () => 'Hello');
```

There's a method for each HTTP method: `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, plus `match` and `any`. A returned string is sent as HTML. A returned array or model is sent as **JSON**, a text format for data that programs read, like `{"id": 5, "title": "Hi"}`.

- **Parameters**: `/posts/{id}` passes that part of the URL to your function as `$id`; `{slug?}` is optional and needs a default value. Restrict it with `->whereNumber('id')`.
- **Named routes**: `->name('posts.show')`, then build URLs with `route('posts.show', ['id' => 5])`. Never type URLs by hand in your pages; if a path changes, named routes keep working.
- **Groups** share settings: `Route::prefix('admin')->middleware('auth')->group(function () { ... })` puts `/admin` in front of every URL inside and requires a logged-in user.
- **Resource routes**: `Route::resource('photos', PhotoController::class)` registers the seven standard routes for listing, showing, creating, editing and deleting photos (`index`, `create`, `store`, `show`, `edit`, `update`, `destroy`); `apiResource` leaves out the two that show forms.

**Route model binding** saves a lot of code. Give a parameter a model class as its type — a class that stands for one database table, covered in the Eloquent lesson — and the same name as the URL part. Laravel then loads that record for you, or answers 404 Not Found if it doesn't exist:

```php
Route::get('/users/{user}', fn (User $user) => $user);
```

Use `{post:slug}` to look the record up by another column. `php artisan route:list` shows every route.
concepts.code:
<?php
// routes/web.php
use App\Http\Controllers\PhotoController;
use App\Models\Post;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/', fn () => view('welcome'))->name('home');

Route::get('/greet/{name?}', fn (string $name = 'guest') => "Hello, $name")
    ->where('name', '[A-Za-z]+');

// /posts/my-first-post -> Post found by slug, or 404
Route::get('/posts/{post:slug}', fn (Post $post) => $post)->name('posts.show');

Route::resource('photos', PhotoController::class);
// GET /photos, GET /photos/create, POST /photos, GET /photos/{photo},
// GET /photos/{photo}/edit, PUT/PATCH /photos/{photo}, DELETE /photos/{photo}

Route::prefix('admin')->middleware('auth')->name('admin.')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/stats', fn () => ['users' => 42])->name('stats');   // admin.stats
});

// route('posts.show', $post) -> https://example.test/posts/my-first-post
takeaways: Each HTTP method has a Route method; return a string, a view, or data that becomes JSON
Name routes and build URLs with route()
Model parameters are loaded automatically (404 if missing)
pitfalls: Typing URLs by hand in pages instead of using named routes, which breaks when paths change.

quiz.q: What does Route::get('/users/{user}', fn (User $user) => $user) do for /users/999 if no such user exists?
quiz.explain: Route model binding looks the user up and answers 404 Not Found when there's no match.

concepts.name: Controllers and requests
concepts.summary: Move route code into controller classes, read input from the Request object, and return pages, redirects or JSON.
concepts.why: Controllers keep route files small and give each part of the app a clear home.
concepts.body:
As an app grows, putting all the code in `routes/web.php` gets messy. A **controller** is a class that groups the code for one part of the app: `PostController` handles blog posts, with one method per action (list posts, show one, save one). Generate one with `php artisan make:controller PostController`; add `--resource` to get empty methods for all seven resource routes.

Wire it up with `Route::get('/posts', [PostController::class, 'index']);`. A controller with a single `__invoke` method can be routed directly: `Route::post('/checkout', CheckoutController::class);`.

Controller methods ask for what they need through their parameter types. Laravel sees `Request $request` or `Post $post` and passes in the right objects, along with route parameters. That's dependency injection, done for you by Laravel's service container (a later lesson):

```php
public function update(Request $request, Post $post) { ... }
```

The `Illuminate\Http\Request` object holds everything about the request:
- `$request->input('title')` reads a value sent by the browser, from the query string or a submitted form (or JSON), with an optional default; `$request->query('page')` reads only the query string.
- `$request->only(['title', 'body'])`, `has('x')`, `filled('x')`, `boolean('remember')`, `integer('page')`.
- `$request->file('avatar')`, `$request->user()`, `$request->ip()`, `$request->isMethod('post')`.

Whatever a method returns becomes the response:
- `view('posts.index', ['posts' => $posts])` builds an HTML page from a **template**, a page with blanks Laravel fills in (next lesson).
- An array, a model or `response()->json($data, 201)` produces JSON.
- `abort(403)` stops with an error page (403 means Forbidden).

To send the user to another page, for example after saving a form, return a **redirect**: a response telling the browser to load a different URL. `redirect()->route('posts.show', $post)->with('status', 'Saved!')` also attaches a one-time **flash message**. It's kept in the user's **session**, the server's memory of one visitor, for just the next page.

Keep controllers thin: check the input, call a model or another class to do the work, return a response.
concepts.code:
<?php
namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Post;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
class PostController extends Controller
{
    public function index(Request $request)
    {
        $posts = Post::query()
            ->when($request->query('q'), fn ($q, $term) => $q->where('title', 'like', "%{$term}%"))
            ->latest()
            ->paginate(10);
        return view('posts.index', ['posts' => $posts]);
    }
    public function show(Post $post)
    {
        return request()->wantsJson() ? $post : view('posts.show', compact('post'));
    }
    public function destroy(Post $post)
    {
        $post->delete();
        return redirect()->route('posts.index')->with('status', 'Post deleted');
    }
}
takeaways: Route to [Controller::class, 'method'] or to an invokable controller
Declare Request, models and services as parameters and Laravel passes them in
Return a view, a redirect, an array or model (JSON), or a response() object
pitfalls: Putting business logic and queries for several features into one giant controller.

quiz.q: What does a controller method that returns an Eloquent model produce?
quiz.explain: Laravel converts models and arrays returned from routes or controllers into JSON.

concepts.name: Blade templates and components
concepts.summary: Build HTML pages with Blade: safe output, @if and @foreach, reusable components with slots, and forms with @csrf.
concepts.why: Blade is how Laravel builds the HTML pages it sends to browsers, safely and from reusable pieces.
concepts.body:
**Blade** is Laravel's template language: HTML with blanks and simple commands that Laravel fills in with your data. Templates live in `resources/views` and end in `.blade.php`; `view('posts.show', [...])` uses `resources/views/posts/show.blade.php`. Laravel turns each template into plain PHP once and reuses the result, so it's fast. Output: - `{{ $post->title }}` prints a value **escaped**: characters like `<` become harmless text, so a user can't sneak HTML or scripts into your page (an XSS attack). - `{!! $html !!}` prints raw HTML; use it only for content you trust. **Directives** are Blade commands starting with `@` that stand for PHP control structures: `@if`/`@elseif`/`@else`/`@endif`, `@unless`, `@isset`, `@foreach`, and `@forelse ... @empty ... @endforelse` for lists that may be empty. Inside loops, `$loop->first`, `$loop->last` and `$loop->iteration` are available. `@auth`/`@guest` show something only to logged-in users or only to visitors; `@can('update', $post)` only to users allowed to do that action. Reuse page pieces with **components**. A simple component is just a view in `resources/views/components`, used like an HTML tag: ```blade

All posts

 ``` Inside `components/layout.blade.php`, `{{ $slot }}` prints whatever was placed between the tags (the **slot**), and `$title` the value given as `title="..."`. Named slots use ``. Class-based components (`php artisan make:component Alert`) add PHP logic. Forms that change data need `@csrf`. It adds a hidden CSRF token, a random code that Laravel checks on every POST, so other websites can't submit forms in your user's name (**CSRF**, cross-site request forgery). **HTML forms** (a page's input boxes and its submit button) can only send GET or POST, so add `@method('PUT')` to say you mean PUT, PATCH or DELETE. Show validation errors with `@error('title') {{ $message }} @enderror` and refill the inputs with `old('title')`.
takeaways: {{ }} escapes output; {!! !!} doesn't, so use it rarely
Components (<x-name>) with $slot replace copy-pasted layouts
Every form needs @csrf; use @method for PUT/PATCH/DELETE
pitfalls: Printing user content with {!! !!}, which opens an XSS hole.

quiz.q: A POST form in a Blade view returns HTTP 419. What is most likely missing?
quiz.explain: 419 means the CSRF token was missing or expired; @csrf adds it to the form.

concepts.name: Migrations and schema
concepts.summary: Create and change database tables with migrations, links between tables and indexes, and run or undo them with Artisan.
concepts.why: Migrations keep your database structure in your code, so every developer and server ends up with exactly the same tables.
concepts.code:
<?php
// database/migrations/2025_06_01_000000_create_posts_table.php
use Illuminate\Database\Migrations\Migration;
use Illuminate\Database\Schema\Blueprint;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schema;
return new class extends Migration
{
    public function up(): void
    {
        Schema::create('posts', function (Blueprint $table) {
            $table->id();
            $table->foreignId('user_id')->constrained()->cascadeOnDelete();
            $table->string('title');
            $table->string('slug')->unique();
            $table->text('body');
            $table->timestamp('published_at')->nullable()->index();
            $table->timestamps();
        });
    }
    public function down(): void
    {
        Schema::dropIfExists('posts');
    }
};
// $ php artisan migrate   ->   2025_06_01_000000_create_posts_table ... DONE
takeaways: Each migration has up() and down() and runs once per database
foreignId()->constrained() creates the column and the foreign key
Write new migrations instead of editing ones that already ran
pitfalls: Running migrate:fresh against a shared or production database, which drops all tables.

quiz.q: A teammate's migration already ran in production but has a typo in a column name. What should you do?
options: Write a new migration that renames the column
Change the column by hand in production
Edit the migration file and redeploy
quiz.explain: Ran migrations are never re-run, so changes must come from a new migration.

concepts.name: Eloquent models and queries
concepts.summary: Define Eloquent models, query them with chained methods, and create, update and delete records safely.
concepts.why: Eloquent is how almost every Laravel app reads and writes its data.
concepts.body:
**Eloquent** is Laravel's **ORM**: it lets you work with database rows as PHP objects instead of writing SQL. An **Eloquent model** is a class in `app/Models` that stands for one table: by convention `Post` uses the `posts` table, `id` is the primary key, and the `created_at`/`updated_at` columns are filled in automatically.

You query through the model with the **query builder**: methods you chain one after another, each adding a piece of the SQL query:

```php
$posts = Post::where('published', true)->orderByDesc('created_at')->take(10)->get();
```

- `get()` returns a **Collection** (Laravel's more capable array) of models; `first()` one model or null; `find($id)` by primary key; `findOrFail($id)` throws an exception when nothing is found, which Laravel turns into a 404 page.
- `count()`, `exists()`, `pluck('title')`, `paginate(15)`.
- `where('votes', '>', 100)`, `whereIn`, `whereNull`, `orWhere`, and `when($cond, fn ($q) => ...)` for optional filters.

All values are sent to the database separately from the SQL text, as PDO prepared-statement parameters, so they're safe from SQL injection.

Writing data:
- `Post::create([...])` inserts a row and returns the model; `$post->update([...])` changes it; `$post->delete()` removes it.
- Or set properties and call `$post->save()`.
- `firstOrCreate` and `updateOrCreate` handle "find it, or insert it" cases.

`create` and `update` fill many columns at once from an array (**mass assignment**), so the model must list which columns may be filled that way: `protected $fillable = ['title', 'body'];` (or list forbidden ones in `$guarded`). Otherwise a malicious visitor could add an extra value such as `is_admin` to a form and make themselves an administrator.

Define **casts** in a `casts()` method to turn column values into proper PHP types when you read them: `'published_at' => 'datetime'` gives a date object, `'options' => 'array'` decodes stored JSON into an array, and `'status' => Status::class` gives an enum.
concepts.code:
<?php
namespace App\Models;

use App\Enums\Status;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;

class Post extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = ['title', 'slug', 'body', 'status', 'published_at'];
    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return ['published_at' => 'datetime', 'status' => Status::class];
    }
}

// Usage (e.g. in php artisan tinker):
$post = Post::create(['title' => 'Hi', 'slug' => 'hi', 'body' => '...', 'status' => 'draft']);
$post->update(['status' => Status::Published, 'published_at' => now()]);
$recent = Post::where('status', Status::Published)
    ->where('published_at', '>=', now()->subWeek())
    ->latest('published_at')
    ->get();                                  // Collection of Post models
$titles = $recent->pluck('title');            // Collection of strings
$post->published_at->diffForHumans();         // "1 second ago" (dates are Carbon objects)
Post::findOrFail(999);                        // ModelNotFoundException -> 404
takeaways: One model per table; conventions decide table and key names
Chain where/orderBy/take and finish with get, first, find or paginate
List columns in $fillable for mass assignment; use casts() for types
pitfalls: Calling Post::create($request->all()) with a broad $guarded = [], letting users set any column.

quiz.q: Why does Post::create($request->all()) ignore an is_admin field sent by the client?
options: is_admin is not in $fillable, so mass assignment skips it
quiz.explain: Only attributes listed in $fillable (or not in $guarded) can be mass-assigned.

concepts.name: Validation and form requests
concepts.summary: Check input with $request->validate and Form Request classes, and show errors to users or to programs that send JSON.
concepts.why: Never trusting input is rule one of web development, and Laravel lets you list the rules instead of writing the checks.
concepts.body:
The quickest way is `$request->validate()` in a controller:

```php
$data = $request->validate([
    'title' => ['required', 'string', 'max:255'],
    'email' => ['required', 'email', 'unique:users,email'],
    'tags' => ['array'], 'tags.*' => ['string', 'distinct'],
]);
```

If validation passes, it returns **only the checked values**, safe to pass to `create()`. If it fails, Laravel throws a `ValidationException` and answers for you. For a regular form submission it redirects back to the form, with the error messages and the user's input flashed to the session (shown with `@error` and `old()`). For a request that expects JSON, such as one from a mobile app, it returns a **422** response with an `errors` object.

For anything non-trivial, use a **Form Request** class: `php artisan make:request StorePostRequest`. It has `rules()` and `authorize()` (may this user do this at all?), and runs automatically when a controller method declares it as a parameter type, so the controller stays tiny. Read the clean data with `$request->validated()`.

Useful rules: `required`, `nullable`, `sometimes`, `string`, `integer`, `numeric`, `boolean`, `in:a,b`, `min`/`max`/`between`, `date`, `after:today`, `confirmed`, `exists:table,column`, `file`, `image`, `mimes:pdf`. Build complex ones with the `Rule` class, for example `Rule::unique('users')->ignore($user->id)` when updating, `Rule::enum(Status::class)` and `Password::min(12)->letters()->numbers()`. Custom rule objects come from `make:rule`.
concepts.code:
<?php
namespace App\Http\Requests;

use App\Enums\Status;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;
use Illuminate\Validation\Rule;
class UpdatePostRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function authorize(): bool
    {
        return $this->user()->can('update', $this->route('post'));
    }
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'title' => ['required', 'string', 'max:255'],
            'slug' => ['required', 'alpha_dash', Rule::unique('posts')->ignore($this->route('post'))],
            'status' => ['required', Rule::enum(Status::class)],
            'published_at' => ['nullable', 'date', 'after_or_equal:today'],
        ];
    }
}
// PostController@update(UpdatePostRequest $request, Post $post):
//     $post->update($request->validated());
// Bad JSON input -> 422 {"message": "...", "errors": {"title": ["..."]}}
takeaways: validate() returns only the checked data, safe for create/update
Failures redirect back with errors, or return 422 JSON to programs that ask for JSON
Form Requests hold `rules()` and `authorize()` outside the controller
pitfalls: Validating but then saving $request->all() instead of the validated data.

quiz.q: A mobile app sends JSON with Accept: application/json and fails validation. What does it receive?
options: A 422 response with an errors object
quiz.explain: When the request expects JSON, ValidationException is rendered as a 422 JSON response.

concepts.name: Relationships and eager loading
concepts.summary: Define hasMany, belongsTo and belongsToMany relationships, and avoid the N+1 query problem with eager loading.
concepts.why: Relationships connect your models the way foreign keys connect tables, and N+1 queries are the most common Laravel performance problem.
concepts.body:
Relationships are methods on models that return relationship objects:

- `hasMany`/`belongsTo`: a `User` has many `Post`s (through `posts.user_id`), and each Post belongs to a User.
- `hasOne`; `belongsToMany` for many-to-many links, such as posts and tags, stored in a **pivot table** like `post_tag` that holds pairs of ids (manage it with `attach`, `detach` and `sync`); `hasManyThrough`; and **polymorphic relationships** (`morphMany`/`morphTo`), where one table such as `comments` can belong to several kinds of model, such as posts and videos.

Use a relationship as a **property** to get the results (`$user->posts` is a Collection, loaded once and then kept on the model), or as a **method** to keep querying: `$user->posts()->where('published', true)->count()`. Create related rows through it: `$user->posts()->create([...])` fills in `user_id` for you.

The **N+1 problem**: looping over 50 posts and printing `$post->author->name` runs 1 query for the posts plus 50 more, one per author. Fix it with **eager loading**: say up front which relationships you'll need, and Eloquent fetches each with one extra query:

```php
$posts = Post::with(['author', 'tags'])->latest()->get();   // 3 queries total
```

- `with('comments.author')` loads nested relationships; filter them with `with(['comments' => fn ($q) => $q->latest()])`.
- `load('author')` eager-loads onto models you already have.
- `withCount('comments')` adds a `comments_count` value without loading the rows; `whereHas('comments', ...)` filters by related rows.

Loading a relationship only when it's first used, as in the slow loop above, is called lazy loading. Add `Model::preventLazyLoading(! app()->isProduction());` in `AppServiceProvider::boot` so lazy loading throws an error during development and N+1 problems show up immediately.
concepts.code:
<?php
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Relations\{BelongsTo, BelongsToMany, HasMany};

class Post extends Model
{
    public function author(): BelongsTo { return $this->belongsTo(User::class, 'user_id'); }
    public function comments(): HasMany { return $this->hasMany(Comment::class); }
    public function tags(): BelongsToMany { return $this->belongsToMany(Tag::class)->withTimestamps(); }
}

// N+1: 1 query + 1 per post
foreach (Post::all() as $post) echo $post->author->name;

// Eager loaded: 3 queries no matter how many posts
$posts = Post::with(['author', 'tags'])
    ->withCount('comments')                         // adds comments_count
    ->whereHas('tags', fn ($q) => $q->where('name', 'laravel'))
    ->latest()->get();
foreach ($posts as $p) echo "{$p->title} by {$p->author->name} ({$p->comments_count})";

$post->tags()->sync([1, 3]);                        // pivot rows now exactly 1 and 3
$user->posts()->create(['title' => 'Hi']);          // user_id set automatically
takeaways: Relationship as property = loaded results; as method = a query you can extend
with() eager-loads relationships with one query each, fixing N+1
preventLazyLoading in development surfaces N+1 problems early
pitfalls: Calling $post->comments()->count() inside a loop; use withCount on the parent query.

quiz.q: Listing 100 posts with each author's name, how many queries does Post::with('author')->get() need?
quiz.explain: One query for posts and one WHERE id IN (...) query for all their authors.

concepts.name: Middleware
concepts.summary: Filter and modify requests with middleware, register it in bootstrap/app.php, and apply it to routes and groups.
concepts.why: Checking who is logged in, rejecting forged forms, limiting how often someone may call you, and logging all run as middleware around your controllers.
concepts.code:
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/AddRequestId.php
namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Str;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
class AddRequestId
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        $id = $request->header('X-Request-Id') ?? (string) Str::uuid();
        $request->attributes->set('request_id', $id);      // before
        $response = $next($request);
        $response->headers->set('X-Request-Id', $id);       // after
        return $response;
    }
}
// bootstrap/app.php
// ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware) {
//     $middleware->append(AddRequestId::class);           // every request
//     $middleware->alias(['subscribed' => EnsureUserIsSubscribed::class]);
// })
// routes/web.php: Route::get('/reports', ...)->middleware(['auth', 'subscribed', 'throttle:30,1']);
takeaways: Middleware runs before and after the handler around $next($request)
Register globally, in groups or by alias in bootstrap/app.php
Built-ins include auth, throttle, can and signed
pitfalls: Forgetting to return $next($request), which ends the request with an empty response.

quiz.q: In a middleware, where do you put code that must modify the outgoing response?
options: After $next($request) returns, before returning the response
quiz.explain: $next($request) returns the response from inner layers, which you can then modify.

concepts.name: Authentication and authorization
concepts.summary: Log users in with Laravel's auth system or a starter kit, protect routes, and authorize actions with gates and policies.
concepts.why: Every app needs to know who the user is and what they may do, and getting either wrong lets strangers into other people's data.
concepts.body:
**Authentication** answers "who are you?", usually by logging in. The fastest start is a starter kit, which generates login, registration, password-reset and email-verification pages. Underneath it uses a few calls you can make yourself:

- `Auth::attempt(['email' => $e, 'password' => $p], $remember)` checks the email and password. Passwords are never stored as typed: the `hashed` cast on the User model stores a **hash**, a scrambled fingerprint that can be checked but not turned back into the password.
- `auth()->user()` or `$request->user()` returns the logged-in user; `Auth::check()` tells you whether anyone is logged in.
- Protect routes with the `auth` middleware; visitors who aren't logged in are sent to the `login` route.

Laravel remembers who is logged in through the **session**, the server's memory of one visitor, linked to their browser by a **cookie** (a small value the browser sends back with every request). After a successful login, call `$request->session()->regenerate()` to give the session a new ID, so an attacker who planted a known ID beforehand can't take it over (**session fixation**). On logout call `Auth::logout()`, then `invalidate()` the session and `regenerateToken()` for a fresh CSRF token.

For mobile apps and JavaScript front ends, **Sanctum** issues API tokens (long random codes the app sends instead of a password), or uses normal cookie-based login for a front end on the same domain.

**Authorization** answers "may you do this?".
- **Gates** are closures for general abilities: `Gate::define('view-reports', fn (User $u) => $u->is_admin);`.
- **Policies** group the rules for one model: `php artisan make:policy PostPolicy --model=Post` creates methods like `update(User $user, Post $post)`. Laravel finds them automatically by their names.

Check permissions with `Gate::authorize('update', $post)` (throws a 403), `$user->can('update', $post)`, the `can:update,post` middleware, or `@can` in Blade. Always check on the server, even if the page hides the button.
concepts.code: id === $post->user_id; } } class SessionController extends Controller { public function store(Request $request) { $credentials = $request->validate(['email' => 'required|email', 'password' => 'required']); if (! Auth::attempt($credentials, $request->boolean('remember'))) { return back()->withErrors(['email' => 'Invalid credentials.'])->onlyInput('email'); } $request->session()->regenerate(); return redirect()->intended('/dashboard'); } } // PostController@update: Gate::authorize('update', $post); // 403 if not allowed // routes/web.php: Route::put('/posts/{post}', ...)->middleware(['auth', 'can:update,post']); // Blade: @can('update', $post) Edit @endcan
takeaways: Auth::attempt logs in; regenerate the session afterwards
Policies hold per-model rules; gates hold general abilities
Authorize on the server with Gate::authorize, can middleware or $user->can
pitfalls: Hiding an Edit button with @can but not checking in the controller, so a hand-made request still works.

quiz.q: Where should the rule "only the author may edit a post" live in Laravel?
quiz.explain: Policies centralise per-model authorization so controllers, routes and views all share it.

concepts.name: Service container and providers
concepts.summary: Let the service container inject dependencies, bind interfaces to implementations and configure services in providers.
concepts.why: The container is the backbone of Laravel: understanding it makes your code testable and the framework predictable.
concepts.body:
The **service container** builds objects for you, along with everything they need. When Laravel calls one of your classes, such as a controller, it reads the types of the constructor and method parameters and builds an object for each — and for each of *their* parameters, all the way down:

```php
public function __construct(private PaymentGateway $payments) {}
```

Classes whose constructor parameters can all be built this way need no setup at all (**auto-wiring**). You only register **bindings**, rules for how to build something, when the container can't work it out alone, typically for an interface:

- `$this->app->bind(PaymentGateway::class, StripeGateway::class)` says which class to build when the interface is asked for, making a new object each time.
- `singleton(...)` builds one shared object (a **singleton**) and hands out the same one every time. `scoped(...)` gives one per request or per background job, which stays safe when the app runs in a long-lived process (see Octane later).
- A closure controls the building: `singleton(Client::class, fn ($app) => new Client(config('services.x.key')))`.
- Contextual binding gives different classes to different users of an interface: `when(ReportController::class)->needs(Filesystem::class)->give(...)`.

Bindings belong in **service providers**, classes that set the app up as it starts (**boots**). `register()` should only add bindings. `boot()` runs after every provider has registered, so it can safely use other services; most app-wide setup goes there. Providers are listed in `bootstrap/providers.php`; `AppServiceProvider` is where most apps start.

Get an object by hand with `app(Foo::class)` or `app()->make(Foo::class)`, but prefer asking for it in the constructor. In tests, `$this->app->instance(PaymentGateway::class, $fake)` swaps in a fake for the whole app.
concepts.code:
<?php
interface PaymentGateway { public function charge(int $cents, string $token): string; }

class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway
{
    public function __construct(private string $secret) {}
    public function charge(int $cents, string $token): string { /* call Stripe */ return 'ch_123'; }
}

// app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php
class AppServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    public function register(): void
    {
        $this->app->singleton(PaymentGateway::class,
            fn ($app) => new StripeGateway(config('services.stripe.secret')));
    }
}
// Auto-wired: no binding needed for CheckoutController itself
class CheckoutController
{
    public function __construct(private PaymentGateway $payments) {}
    public function __invoke(Request $r) { return ['id' => $this->payments->charge(999, $r->input('token'))]; }
}
// In a test: $this->app->instance(PaymentGateway::class, new FakeGateway());
takeaways: The container auto-wires constructor dependencies by their types
Bind interfaces with bind, singleton or scoped in a provider's register()
boot() runs after all providers register and may use other services
pitfalls: Resolving services inside register(), before other providers have registered their bindings.

quiz.q: What is the difference between bind and singleton?
options: bind is for interfaces, singleton for classes
bind makes a new object each time; singleton reuses one object
quiz.explain: singleton keeps the first object it builds and returns it every time; bind builds a fresh one on each request for it.

concepts.name: JSON APIs with resources and Sanctum
concepts.summary: Build JSON APIs with API routes, API resource classes, pagination and Sanctum tokens.
concepts.why: Most Laravel apps also serve mobile apps or JavaScript front ends, and resources keep the JSON stable as models change.
concepts.body:
A **web API** is a set of URLs that other programs, such as a mobile app or a JavaScript front end, call to read or change data as JSON instead of loading pages. Run `php artisan install:api` to add `routes/api.php` (its URLs start with `/api`) and install **Sanctum** for logging in. API routes are **stateless**: no sessions or cookies, so every request must prove who it is by itself.

Returning models directly works, but then your API changes whenever your database columns do. An **API resource** is a class that converts a model into exactly the JSON clients should see: `php artisan make:resource PostResource` creates one, and its `toArray()` decides the shape:

```php
return [
    'id' => $this->id,
    'title' => $this->title,
    'author' => new UserResource($this->whenLoaded('author')),
    'comments_count' => $this->whenCounted('comments'),
];
```

`$this` passes through to the model's own values. `whenLoaded` includes a relationship only if it was already eager-loaded, so a resource never sneaks in extra queries (the N+1 problem). `when($cond, $value)` adds a value only sometimes, for example for admins.

Return `new PostResource($post)` for one item and `PostResource::collection($posts)` for many. Output is wrapped in a `data` key; with a paginator, `links` and `meta` (current page, total and so on) are added automatically. Set status codes with `->response()->setStatusCode(201)`.

**Sanctum tokens**: `$user->createToken('mobile', ['posts:write'])->plainTextToken` creates a **token**, a long random code that works like a password for one app, and shows it once. The client sends it with every request in a header: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Protect routes with the `auth:sanctum` middleware, and check what a token may do with `$request->user()->tokenCan('posts:write')`. For your own JavaScript front end on the same domain, Sanctum can use normal cookie-based login instead.

Limit how often clients may call (the `throttle` middleware), put a version in the path (`/api/v1`), and return errors in one consistent shape.
concepts.code:
<?php
// app/Http/Resources/PostResource.php
class PostResource extends JsonResource
{
    public function toArray(Request $request): array
    {
        return [
            'id' => $this->id,
            'title' => $this->title,
            'author' => new UserResource($this->whenLoaded('author')),
            'comments_count' => $this->whenCounted('comments'),
            'internal_notes' => $this->when($request->user()?->is_admin, $this->notes),
        ];
    }
}

// routes/api.php
Route::middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:60,1'])->prefix('v1')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/posts', fn () => PostResource::collection(
        Post::with('author')->withCount('comments')->latest()->paginate(20)
    ));
    Route::post('/posts', [PostApiController::class, 'store']);
});
// GET /api/v1/posts -> {"data": [...], "links": {...}, "meta": {"current_page": 1, ...}}
// Issue a token: $user->createToken('mobile', ['posts:write'])->plainTextToken
takeaways: API resources separate the JSON shape from database columns
whenLoaded and whenCounted avoid hidden N+1 queries
Sanctum issues tokens sent as `Authorization: Bearer`; protect routes with auth:sanctum
pitfalls: Returning models straight from API routes, leaking new columns (or hidden data) as the schema evolves.

quiz.q: What does whenLoaded('author') do if the author relation wasn't eager-loaded?
options: Omits the key from the output
Returns null and logs a warning
quiz.explain: The attribute is removed from the response, so resources never trigger lazy loading.

concepts.name: Queues and jobs
concepts.summary: Push slow work into queued jobs, run workers, and handle retries, failures, batching and transactions.
concepts.why: Sending email, calling other services and processing files while the user waits makes apps slow and fragile; queues move that work out of the request.
concepts.body:
A **queue** is a waiting line of tasks. A **job** is a class describing one task to do later: `php artisan make:job ProcessPodcast`. It implements `ShouldQueue` and has a `handle()` method, whose parameters the container fills in.

Dispatch it with `ProcessPodcast::dispatch($podcast)`. The job is **serialized** (turned into text) and stored by the queue driver: `database` (the default in new apps), `redis`, `sqs`, `beanstalkd`, or `sync` (runs immediately, handy for tests). A **worker**, a separate long-running PHP process started with `php artisan queue:work`, picks jobs up and runs them. In production, keep workers running with a process manager such as Supervisor or systemd. Workers load your code once and keep it in memory, so after each **deploy** (putting a new version live) run `php artisan queue:restart`.

Models passed to a job are stored as their ids (thanks to `SerializesModels`) and fetched fresh from the database when the job runs.

Reliability controls:
- `public $tries = 5;` and `public $backoff = [10, 60, 300];` set how many **retries** a failing job gets and how many seconds to wait before each, waiting longer each time (**exponential backoff**). `retryUntil()` sets a deadline; `$timeout` stops runaway jobs.
- `failed(Throwable $e)` runs after the final failure; failed jobs land in the `failed_jobs` table (`queue:failed`, `queue:retry all`).
- Make jobs **idempotent**, safe to run twice with the same result, since a job can run more than once.

Dispatching inside a database transaction is risky: the worker may run before the commit and not find the row. Use `->afterCommit()` or the `after_commit` connection option.

Extras: `->delay(now()->addMinutes(10))`, `->onQueue('emails')`, `Bus::chain([...])` for jobs that must run in order, `Bus::batch([...])` for groups with progress tracking and callbacks, `ShouldBeUnique`, and rate-limiting job middleware. **Horizon** gives Redis queues a dashboard and balances workers automatically.
concepts.code:
<?php
// app/Jobs/GenerateInvoicePdf.php
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Queue\Queueable;

class GenerateInvoicePdf implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Queueable;
    public int $tries = 4;
    public array $backoff = [10, 60, 300];      // seconds between attempts
    public function __construct(public Invoice $invoice) {}   // stored as an id
    public function handle(PdfRenderer $pdf): void            // injected
    {
        if ($this->invoice->pdf_path) return;                  // idempotent
        $path = $pdf->render('invoices.show', ['invoice' => $this->invoice]);
        $this->invoice->update(['pdf_path' => $path]);
    }
    public function failed(Throwable $e): void
    {
        $this->invoice->owner->notify(new InvoiceFailed($this->invoice));
    }
}
// Controller: respond fast, work later (after the transaction commits)
GenerateInvoicePdf::dispatch($invoice)->onQueue('pdfs')->afterCommit();
// $ php artisan queue:work --queue=pdfs,default --tries=4
takeaways: Jobs implement ShouldQueue and are processed by queue:work workers
Configure tries, backoff and failed(); design jobs to be idempotent
Dispatch after commit and restart workers on deploy
pitfalls: Deploying new code without queue:restart, so long-running workers keep executing the old version.

quiz.q: Why use ->afterCommit() when dispatching a job inside a DB transaction?
options: So the worker can't run before the data it needs is committed
It makes the job run faster
quiz.explain: Without it a fast worker may query rows that the still-open transaction hasn't committed yet.

concepts.name: Events, listeners and observers
concepts.summary: Separate follow-up work with events and listeners, run listeners on the queue, and react to model changes with observers.
concepts.why: Events keep controllers focused while features like notifications, activity logs and analytics plug in.
concepts.body:
An **event** is a plain class describing something that happened, such as `OrderShipped`. **Listeners** react to it. This decouples the code that causes an action from everything that should follow: the shipping code doesn't need to know about emails, analytics or webhooks (messages your app sends to another service's URL when something happens).

Create them with `php artisan make:event OrderShipped` and `php artisan make:listener SendShipmentEmail --event=OrderShipped`. Laravel **discovers listeners automatically**: any listener in `app/Listeners` whose `handle` method takes an event class as its parameter type is registered for it. You can also register explicitly with `Event::listen()` in a service provider.

Fire an event with `OrderShipped::dispatch($order)` or `event(new OrderShipped($order))`.

- A listener that implements `ShouldQueue` runs on the queue, so slow follow-up work doesn't delay the response. It supports the same options as jobs (tries, backoff, queue name).
- Implement `ShouldDispatchAfterCommit` on the event (or `ShouldQueueAfterCommit` on a listener) so nothing reacts to data that might be rolled back.

**Model events** fire automatically: `creating`, `created`, `updating`, `updated`, `saving`, `saved`, `deleting`, `deleted` and more. Group handlers in an **observer** (`php artisan make:observer PostObserver --model=Post`) and attach it with the `#[ObservedBy(PostObserver::class)]` attribute on the model.

Be careful: model events don't fire for mass updates like `Post::where(...)->update([...])`, because no models are loaded. Overusing events makes the flow of a program hard to follow, so keep them for genuine **side effects**: extra work an action causes beyond its main job.
concepts.code:
<?php
class OrderShipped implements ShouldDispatchAfterCommit
{
    use Dispatchable, SerializesModels;
    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}
}

// Listener: auto-discovered from the handle() type-hint
class SendShipmentEmail implements ShouldQueue
{
    public function handle(OrderShipped $e): void { Mail::to($e->order->customer)->send(new ShipmentMail($e->order)); }
}
#[ObservedBy(OrderObserver::class)]
class Order extends Model {}
class OrderObserver
{
    public function updated(Order $order): void
    {
        if ($order->wasChanged('status')) AuditLog::record($order, 'status');   // audit trail
    }
}
DB::transaction(function () use ($order) {
    $order->update(['status' => 'shipped']);
    OrderShipped::dispatch($order);   // delivered only after commit
});
takeaways: Events describe what happened; listeners decide what follows
Queued listeners keep follow-up work off the request
Observers handle model lifecycle events, but mass updates skip them
pitfalls: Relying on an observer's updated hook while using query-builder mass updates, which fire no model events.

quiz.q: Does Post::where('draft', true)->update(['draft' => false]) trigger PostObserver::updated?
options: No, mass updates run a single query without loading models
quiz.explain: Model events need model instances; a query-builder update bypasses them.

concepts.name: Testing Laravel apps
concepts.summary: Write feature tests with HTTP helpers, factories, RefreshDatabase, actingAs and fakes for queued jobs, mail and events.
concepts.why: Laravel's testing tools make full-stack tests fast to write, which is what keeps large apps shippable.
concepts.body:
Laravel apps ship ready for testing with **Pest** or **PHPUnit** (you choose when creating the app). Run `php artisan test`. **Feature tests** in `tests/Feature` start the whole app and send it pretend HTTP requests; unit tests in `tests/Unit` test single classes on their own. `phpunit.xml` points tests at an SQLite database held in memory, which is fast and thrown away afterwards.

Key tools:

- `use RefreshDatabase;` migrates once and wraps each test in a transaction that's rolled back, so every test starts clean.
- **Factories** create realistic models: `User::factory()->create()`, `Post::factory()->count(3)->for($user)->create()`, with **states** like `->unverified()`.
- HTTP helpers: `$this->get('/posts')`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, and JSON variants `postJson` and `getJson`.
- Assertions on the response: `assertOk()`, `assertStatus(201)`, `assertRedirect()`, `assertSee('Title')`, `assertJsonPath('data.0.id', 1)`, `assertInvalid(['title'])`, `assertForbidden()`.
- `actingAs($user)` authenticates a request.
- Database assertions: `assertDatabaseHas('posts', [...])`, `assertDatabaseCount`, `assertModelMissing`.

**Fakes** replace actions with side effects, such as sending mail or pushing a job onto the queue, with recorders: `Queue::fake()` then `Queue::assertPushed(SendInvoice::class)`; `Mail::fake()`, `Notification::fake()`, `Event::fake()`, `Storage::fake('s3')`, `Http::fake([...])` for outgoing HTTP calls. `$this->freezeTime()` or `travel(5)->days()` control the clock.

Test most features through their URLs (their **endpoints**), and keep unit tests for complex business rules.
concepts.code:
<?php
// tests/Feature/PublishPostTest.php
use App\Jobs\NotifySubscribers;
use App\Models\{Post, User};
use Illuminate\Foundation\Testing\RefreshDatabase;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Queue;

class PublishPostTest extends \Tests\TestCase
{
    use RefreshDatabase;

    public function test_author_can_publish_and_subscribers_are_notified(): void
    {
        Queue::fake();
        $author = User::factory()->create();
        $post = Post::factory()->for($author, 'author')->create(['status' => 'draft']);
        $this->actingAs($author)
            ->putJson("/api/v1/posts/{$post->id}/publish")
            ->assertOk()
            ->assertJsonPath('data.status', 'published');
        $this->assertDatabaseHas('posts', ['id' => $post->id, 'status' => 'published']);
        Queue::assertPushed(NotifySubscribers::class, fn ($job) => $job->post->is($post));
    }
    // + a test that another user gets ->assertForbidden()
}
takeaways: RefreshDatabase plus factories give each test a clean, realistic database
HTTP test helpers and actingAs exercise routes end to end
Queue, Mail, Event, Http and Storage fakes record side effects for assertions
pitfalls: Calling real outside services in tests instead of using Http::fake(), making the suite slow and flaky (randomly failing).

quiz.q: What does Queue::fake() do in a test?
options: Disables dispatching and throws on dispatch
Records dispatched jobs without running them, so you can assert on them
quiz.explain: The fake captures pushed jobs; assertPushed and assertNotPushed then inspect them.

concepts.name: Large datasets and query performance
concepts.summary: Process big tables with chunkById, lazy and cursor, inspect generated SQL, and keep queries and memory under control.
concepts.why: Code that works on 100 rows can run out of memory or take far too long on 10 million; these tools prevent that.
concepts.body:
`Model::all()` and `get()` load every row into memory as full Eloquent models. For batch work over big tables, handle the rows a piece at a time instead:

- `chunkById(1000, function ($users) { ... })` fetches pages ordered by id using `where id > last_id`, which is fast and stays correct even if you update rows while iterating. Plain `chunk()` uses offsets, which get slower on deep pages and can skip rows when the loop modifies the filtered column.
- `lazyById(1000)` does the same but returns a `LazyCollection` you can `each`, `filter` and `map` like a normal collection.
- `cursor()` runs one query and hydrates models one at a time using a PHP generator. It has the lowest model memory, but the database driver may still hold the whole result in memory, and eager loading isn't possible.

Do less work per row: `select(['id', 'email'])` only the columns you need, use `pluck()` or `value()` for single columns, and push set-based work to the database with query-builder `update()`, `increment()`, `insert()` and `upsert()` (insert or update in one statement) instead of saving models one by one.

See what Eloquent sends: `->toRawSql()` prints SQL with bindings, `->explain()` shows the **query plan** (how the database intends to run the query), and `DB::listen()`, Telescope, Pulse or Debugbar log queries and timings. Look for missing **indexes** on columns used in `where`, `orderBy` and joins, and add them in a migration.

`DB::transaction()` wraps related writes; long-running batch jobs should commit in reasonably small chunks to avoid long locks.
concepts.code:
<?php
use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

// Bad: loads every user into memory at once
// User::all()->each(fn ($u) => ...);

// Keyset pagination: constant memory, safe while updating rows
User::where('active', false)->chunkById(1000, function ($users) {
    User::whereKey($users->modelKeys())->update(['archived_at' => now()]);
});
// LazyCollection pipeline over a big table
$emails = User::select(['id', 'email'])->lazyById(2000)
    ->filter(fn ($u) => str_ends_with($u->email, '@example.com'))
    ->map->email;
foreach ($emails as $email) { /* stream to a CSV, etc. */ }
// Inspect the SQL and plan
echo User::where('email', 'a@b.io')->toRawSql();
// select * from "users" where "email" = 'a@b.io'
dump(User::where('email', 'a@b.io')->explain());
// Set-based write instead of N model saves
DB::table('products')->upsert(
    [['sku' => 'A1', 'price' => 10], ['sku' => 'B2', 'price' => 12]],
    uniqueBy: ['sku'], update: ['price']
);
takeaways: chunkById and lazyById stream big tables with keyset pagination
Select only needed columns and prefer set-based update, insert and upsert
Use toRawSql, explain and query logs to find slow queries and missing indexes
pitfalls: Using chunk() while updating the column you filter on, which silently skips rows.

quiz.q: Why is chunkById safer than chunk when the callback updates the rows being filtered?
options: It pages by id > last seen id instead of OFFSET, so changed rows don't shift pages
quiz.explain: Offset-based paging shifts when filtered rows disappear; keyset paging by id doesn't.

concepts.name: The request lifecycle
concepts.summary: Follow a request from public/index.php through start-up, service providers, the middleware pipeline and the router.
concepts.why: Knowing the lifecycle tells you where to hook in, why caching config matters and how to track down odd framework behaviour.
concepts.body:
Every HTTP request enters through `public/index.php`. It loads Composer's autoloader, then `bootstrap/app.php`, which builds the **Application** (the service container) with `Application::configure()->withRouting()->withMiddleware()->withExceptions()->create()`. Finally `$app->handleRequest(Request::capture())` hands the request to the **HTTP kernel**, the object that walks it through start-up, middleware and the router.

The kernel first runs its **bootstrappers**:

- Load the settings in `.env`, unless config is cached.
- Load configuration (from `bootstrap/cache/config.php` if you ran `config:cache`).
- Set up error and exception handling, register facades.
- **Register** all service providers (their `register()` methods), then **boot** them (their `boot()` methods). Deferred providers register only when one of their services is first requested.

The request then passes through the global **middleware pipeline**, a chain of steps where each one hands the request to the next (implemented with `Illuminate\Pipeline\Pipeline`, where each layer is wrapped around the next as a closure). The **router** matches the route, runs the route's middleware group (for example `web`: cookies, session, CSRF, bindings), resolves the controller through the container and calls it. The return value is converted into a Symfony `Response`, which travels back out through the middleware and is sent. Afterwards `terminate()` runs terminable middleware and `defer()`red callbacks.

Under **PHP-FPM**, the usual setup in which PHP starts the app from scratch for every request, all of this happens every time. That's why caching config and routes matters so much, as does **OPcache**, which keeps PHP files ready to run instead of re-reading them. Under Octane (see the production lesson) the start-up happens only once per long-running worker.
concepts.code:
<?php
// public/index.php (simplified)
define('LARAVEL_START', microtime(true));
require __DIR__.'/../vendor/autoload.php';
$app = require_once __DIR__.'/../bootstrap/app.php';
$app->handleRequest(Illuminate\Http\Request::capture());

// bootstrap/app.php
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\{Exceptions, Middleware};
return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
        commands: __DIR__.'/../routes/console.php',
        health: '/up',
    )
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware) {
        $middleware->append(\App\Http\Middleware\AddRequestId::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions) {
        $exceptions->report(fn (PaymentFailed $e) => Log::channel('payments')->error($e));
    })
    ->create();
// Flow: index.php -> bootstrappers -> providers register() -> boot()
//       -> global middleware -> router -> route middleware -> controller -> back out
takeaways: public/index.php -> bootstrap/app.php -> kernel bootstrappers -> providers -> middleware -> router
All providers register before any boots
Under PHP-FPM bootstrapping repeats per request; caches and OPcache cut that cost
pitfalls: Doing heavy work (queries, HTTP calls) in a provider's boot method, which then runs on every request.

quiz.q: At what point do service providers' boot() methods run?
options: After every provider's register() has run, before the request hits middleware
Only when the provider's service is used
quiz.explain: The kernel registers all providers first, then boots them, then dispatches the request through middleware.

concepts.name: Facades and framework internals
concepts.summary: See how facades resolve services from the container, how to fake and swap them, and how macros extend core classes.
concepts.why: Facades are everywhere in Laravel code; knowing they're just container lookups makes testing and tracking down problems straightforward.
concepts.body:
A **facade** like `Cache::get('key')` looks static but isn't. `Cache` extends `Illuminate\Support\Facades\Facade`, and its only job is `getFacadeAccessor()`, returning a container key such as `'cache'`. When you call a static method, PHP's `__callStatic` magic resolves that key from the container (caching the instance) and forwards the call. So `Cache::get()` is equivalent to `app('cache')->get()`.

Consequences:

- Facades are as testable as injected services. `Cache::shouldReceive('get')->andReturn(...)` swaps in a Mockery mock; `Mail::fake()`, `Queue::fake()` and `Storage::fake()` swap in purpose-built fakes. `Facade::swap($instance)` replaces the root.
- The underlying class is listed in the docs' facade reference and in each facade's `@see` and `@method` comments (PHPDoc), which code editors read to offer autocompletion.
- **Real-time facades**: prefix any class's namespace with `Facades\` (`use Facades\App\Services\Geo;`) and Laravel generates a facade for it on the fly.

Helpers such as `cache()`, `config()` and `app()` are the same container lookups in function form. Choose one style per codebase; asking for services in the constructor makes dependencies most visible.

Many core classes are Macroable: you can add your own methods, called **macros**, while the app runs, with `Collection::macro('toCsv', fn () => ...)`, `Str::macro` or `Request::macro`, registered in a provider's `boot()`. Other extension points include your own model casts, and your own cache, queue or file-storage drivers registered with `extend()`, all built on the `Manager` pattern.

Reading framework source is the best way to answer "how does this work?": everything lives in `vendor/laravel/framework/src/Illuminate`.
concepts.code:
<?php
// What a facade boils down to
class Cache extends \Illuminate\Support\Facades\Facade
{
    protected static function getFacadeAccessor(): string { return 'cache'; }
}
// Cache::get('k')  ==  app('cache')->get('k')

// Testing with facades
Cache::shouldReceive('get')->once()->with('rate:eur')->andReturn(1.08);
$this->assertSame(1.08, app(FxService::class)->rate('eur'));

// Real-time facade for your own class
use Facades\App\Services\Geo;          // generated on the fly
Geo::shouldReceive('country')->andReturn('AM');
echo Geo::country('1.2.3.4');              // AM

// Macro: extend a core class (in AppServiceProvider::boot)
use Illuminate\Support\Collection;
Collection::macro('toCsv', function (): string {
    return $this->map(fn ($row) => implode(',', $row))->implode("\n");
});
echo collect([[1, 'a'], [2, 'b']])->toCsv();   // "1,a\n2,b"
takeaways: A facade forwards static calls to a service resolved from the container
Facades can be mocked with shouldReceive or replaced with fakes
Real-time facades and macros extend the framework without forking it
pitfalls: Believing facades are untestable static calls and wrapping every one of them in custom interfaces.

quiz.q: What does Mail::fake() actually replace?
options: The 'mail.manager' instance behind the facade, with a fake that records messages
quiz.explain: Facades resolve their root from the container, so fake() swaps that root for a recording fake.

concepts.name: Production, caching and Octane
concepts.summary: Deploy Laravel safely: build its caches, run workers and the scheduler, and avoid the pitfalls of Octane's long-lived workers.
concepts.why: Most Laravel production incidents come from deployment mistakes, out-of-date caches or data leaking between Octane requests.
concepts.body:
A production deploy typically runs `composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader`, `php artisan migrate --force`, then **`php artisan optimize`**, which caches config, routes, events and views. Afterwards it reloads PHP-FPM (for OPcache) and runs `php artisan queue:restart`.

**Config caching** (one combined settings file, built by `optimize`) has a famous trap: once config is cached, `.env` is no longer loaded, so `env()` calls outside `config/*.php` files return null. Always read settings via `config('services.stripe.key')` in application code.

Other production essentials:

- `APP_DEBUG=false` (detailed error pages would show passwords and keys to visitors) and `APP_ENV=production`.
- Queue workers kept running by Supervisor or systemd, or by Horizon for Redis.
- One **cron** entry (the server's built-in timer for recurring commands) running `php artisan schedule:run` every minute, which drives the scheduled tasks defined in `routes/console.php`; add `->onOneServer()` when you run several servers.
- With several servers, keep sessions, cache and queues in a shared store (Redis or the database), not on each server.
- A **health check** URL, which monitoring tools call to see whether the app is up, is built in at `/up`; `php artisan down --secret=...` puts the site into **maintenance mode**.

**Octane** serves the app from long-lived workers (FrankenPHP, RoadRunner or Swoole). The app boots once and handles thousands of requests, often several times faster. But anything kept in memory now survives from one request to the next:

- Don't give singletons built at start-up the current request, the config or the container itself; they'll keep the first request's values forever. Fetch those per call, or use `scoped` bindings.
- Avoid static arrays that keep growing: that's a **memory leak**, memory that's never given back. Watch memory use and set `--max-requests` so each worker is replaced after a number of requests.

Hosting services such as Laravel Cloud, Forge and Vapor automate much of this.
concepts.code:
# deploy.sh (simplified, zero-downtime tools do the same steps per release)
set -e
php artisan down --render="errors::503" --retry=15
git pull --ff-only
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader --no-interaction
php artisan migrate --force
php artisan optimize            # config, routes, events, views cached
sudo systemctl reload php8.4-fpm   # fresh OPcache
php artisan queue:restart       # workers finish current job, then reload
php artisan up

# crontab: drive the scheduler
# * * * * * cd /var/www/app && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

# Octane alternative to PHP-FPM
# php artisan octane:start --server=frankenphp --workers=8 --max-requests=1000

# Gotcha after config:cache:
#   env('STRIPE_KEY') in a controller -> null
#   config('services.stripe.key')    -> works (read env only inside config/*.php)
takeaways: php artisan optimize caches config, routes, events and views
After config:cache, env() works only inside config files
Octane boots once: avoid request state in singletons and watch memory
pitfalls: Calling env() directly in application code, which returns null once config is cached.

quiz.q: After php artisan config:cache, what does env('APP_NAME') return inside a controller?
options: null, because .env isn't loaded when config is cached
quiz.explain: With cached config Laravel skips loading .env, so env() outside config files returns null (or its default).

quiz.q: Under Octane, a singleton is constructed with the current Request in its constructor. What goes wrong?
options: Every later request sees the first request's data
The singleton is rebuilt each request automatically
quiz.explain: Singletons live for the worker's lifetime, so they keep the request they were built with.
